extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, entomologists, and evolutionary biologists; informed general readers interested in sexual selection in insects
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and interpreting secondary sexual characters (morphology, colour, sounds, odors, and behaviour) in insects, and inferring their functions (combat, ornament, attraction, protection) using comparative and observational evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male horns/mandibles as sexual characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Males of many beetles possess large horns or toothed mandibles, often differing from females.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether such structures are used in fighting or for seizing females (e.g., Lucanus elaphus seizes the female), their great variability in size/structure, and whether they might serve as ornaments (conspicuous, elegant branching, not well adapted for pinching). Examples: Lamellicorns, Lucanidae, Chiasognathus grantii. Anti-pattern: assuming large size implies fighting function without behavioral evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of battle (male combat for females)
rubrics_metrics.description: Males often engage in conflicts for possession of females; fighting behaviour is evidence of sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct observations of conflicts (pushing with rostra, clawing, pinching) and outcomes (larger male usually wins) to infer selection for fighting adaptations. Examples: Leptorhynchus angustatus, stag-beetle experiments, Lethrus cephalotes (pair burrow defence). Note that some species that fight seem ill-fitted for fighting; interpret cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimorphism and compensation among structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Different individuals or sexes may show compensation between structures (one projection large while another reduced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for correlated reduction/augmentation (e.g., upper vs lower horns in Onitis or Bledius; Siagonium male dimorphism with two male morphs). Consider compensation when one structure is reduced in presence of another enlarged; intermediate forms may exist, so strict categories are not always present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament vs functional weapon distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Large, conspicuous structures may function primarily as ornaments rather than as efficient weapons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mechanical effectiveness (e.g., are mandibles able to pinch effectively?) and conspicuousness (elegant branching) to infer ornamental role. Example: some Lucanidae mandibles may be ornamental. Anti-pattern: inferring combat function solely from size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stridulating organ morphology and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Stridulating organs typically comprise a rasp (fine parallel ribs) and a scraper; their anatomical positions vary widely among coleopterous families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess structure (rasp ribs count, presence of scraper) and position (dorsal abdomen, elytra inferior surface, coxa of hind-leg, meso-thorax, pro-pygidium, etc.). Examples and counts: Necrophorus rasps (126–140 ribs), Geotrupes coxa (84 ribs), Cerambyx heros (238 ribs). Variability in position but structural similarity supports homology of function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual dimorphism in stridulating organs
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence, degree, or absence of stridulating organs may differ between sexes, indicating a sexual function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare cleaned abdominal segments under appropriate light to detect ribs and hair coverage; male-only rasps or more developed rasps in males (e.g., Heliopathes gibbus, H. cribratostriatus, Oryctes species) support the hypothesis that stridulation calls or excites females. Be aware of variability and rare cases where both sexes stridulate equally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral contexts of stridulation/sound production
rubrics_metrics.description: Stridulation and other sounds are used in courtship, mutual calling, distress, anger/defense, and to encourage mates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use behavioral observations to connect sound production to mating contexts (e.g., Ageronia feronia during chase, Ateuchus male encouraging female rolling dung balls, Death's-head Sphinx noise after emergence). Distinguish sexual-calling usage from distress/defense by timing and associated behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative method for inferring causes of colour differences
rubrics_metrics.description: When males and females of the same species inhabit the same district and have identical habits, differences in colour are unlikely due to environmental conditions and more likely due to sexual selection or mimicry/warning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare sexes within species and across closely allied species or genera (example Epicalia: nine species males brilliant, females similar to ancestral type). Infer directionality by noting which sex resembles ancestral group coloration. Use multiple related species and natural-history data to reject direct environmental causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern: males more often more brilliant; females retain ancestral type
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general rule, males are the more beautiful and depart more from the group's usual colouring; females of species in a genus often resemble one another more than males do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey species within a genus (Papilio, Junonia, Lycaena) to assess gradations; when females are conservative in colour, male divergence suggests sexual selection. Exceptions exist where females are more brightly coloured than males.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective function of lower wing surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: The lower (ventral) surface of butterfly wings is often cryptic and adapted to conceal the resting insect; this surface is frequently similar in both sexes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe resting posture (wings closed exposing ventral surface) and match to typical resting substrates (bark, leaves). Examples: Kallima resembling a withered leaf; Thecla rubi matching young bramble leaves. Use similarity between sexes on ventral side as evidence of protective adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting bright upper-surface colours
rubrics_metrics.description: Bright, conspicuous dorsal colours are unlikely to be for concealment; possible functions include sexual attraction, warning (aposematism), or mimicry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish cases: when both sexes are brilliant, warning/aposematism or mimicry are plausible; when only males are brightly coloured but sexes share habitat, sexual selection is a more likely explanation. Examples: Gonepteryx (male intense yellow), Anthocharis cardamines (male orange-tips). Consider whether conspicuousness could be indirectly beneficial (e.g., via mimicry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspicuous hind-wings as a decoy escape mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Bright hind-wings may serve as a decoy, attracting predator attacks to the wings rather than the body, facilitating escape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate predator interactions experimentally or observationally (Weir's aviary experiments with Triphaena pronuba where birds struck at wings repeatedly, allowing escape). Consider size and fragility of wings and predator targeting behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex-specific odor/pheromone production
rubrics_metrics.description: Musky odors or scent organs often occur in males and are associated with sexual function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document presence/absence and development of odor-producing structures (e.g., tympaniform vesicles, musky scent in some Sphinx moths), compare sexes; male-limited odor organs support role in mate attraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability and gradation within genera as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Within a genus, sexes may show every gradation from no colour difference to extreme dimorphism; such patterns indicate repeated and variable action of sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple species comparisons to map gradations (Epicalia, Papilio, Junonia, Lycaena). Interpret cases where males resemble ancestral plain type or where colours have been transferred to females, to infer evolutionary transitions (male change vs female change).
